edge_920.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
edge_920.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson).

edge_921.relationship: Descent into Discourse: the linguistic turn in social history criticised as a 'reification of language', with class held to originate in relations of production rather than in discourse; Stedman Jones's languages of class a principal target (1987–90)
edge_921.evidence_note: The book (Temple University Press, 1990) was not read: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and its search-inside service returned HTTP 403. Its wording is taken from an in-period review that quotes it with page numbers: Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992), pp. 311–313, read in full in the journal's PDF. Callinicos quotes Palmer: 'Much writing that appears under the designer label of poststructuralism/post modernism is, quite bluntly, crap' (199); Callinicos describes Palmer's standpoint, in his own words, as 'not that of a defensive empiricism but of a critical, anti-Stalinist Marxism', and quotes the book: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (xiii); yet discourse theory 'contains insights and guides capable of opening new doors of understanding to historians committed to a materialism that recognizes the need for a rigorous reading of documents and texts/contexts' (189). The book is 'a critical survey of "the reification of language"' from the Russian Formalists through Foucault and Derrida that 'traces the vulgarization of their ideas by historians working in the fields of politics, gender, and class' (p. 312). Against 'the reduction by Gareth Stedman Jones et al. of class as a discursive construct', Palmer writes that 'class relations are, in origin, economic relations rooted in the capitalist process of accumulation, whereby one social stratum expropriates surplus from another' (138) (p. 312). Callinicos's in-period objections: Palmer is 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received in the English-speaking world' and misreads Foucault's Archaeology (p. 312); his claim that 'class as an objective economic reality is not present before the arrival of industrial capitalism' (139) sits oddly with Ste Croix; 'Perhaps, like Edward Thompson before him, Palmer has reacted to the dissolution of agency into structure by underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action' (p. 313). He calls the results 'admirable' and his disagreements 'relatively minor' (p. 312). The target was already set in 1987: Palmer's ILWCH response (p. 14 and n. 2, read) borrows phrases from Stedman Jones's Languages of Class for the first-person scene that opens it, and Scott's reply says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (ILWCH 32, p. 41). Later readings, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer in 1993 granting that 'Poststructurally inclined historians rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted; unread here); Finkel (2021) calls the book Palmer's 'anger with the discursive turn'. Scope: a critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of class, not of attention to language as such. edge_105 (language → social) and edge_200 (historyworkshop–language) stay.

edge_1127.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that insisting on class as the best way to analyse inequality forecloses other political categories and other ways of writing critical history (2000, in her abstract)
edge_1127.evidence_note: Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.

Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class; The Chartists; Work, Culture, and Society

strands.title: Community, culture, and collective action
strands.focus: Davis’s social/cultural inquiry and Tilly’s repertoires connect collective processes with meanings through different scales and methods.
strands.works: “The Rites of Violence” (1973); Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); The Contentious French (1986)

strands.title: Population and household reconstruction
strands.focus: Demographic reconstruction is one important component of the wider field.
strands.works: Cambridge Group population and household studies

strands.title: Mobility, property and linked lives
strands.focus: Separate occupational mobility from savings and property using linked local evidence; representativeness is a historical problem.
strands.works: Poverty and Progress (1964)

strands.title: Gender, family and middle-class formation
strands.focus: Study religious commitments, family arrangements, gender and economic opportunities together in selected English settings.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987)

strands.title: Colonial labor and contested categories
strands.focus: Chakrabarty questions universal class narratives through Bengal jute workers; Cooper examines colonial labor classifications and African social relations. Neither supplies one model for all colonized workers.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Experience, identities and historical explanation
strands.focus: Read Scott’s critique of foundational experience alongside Thompson’s historical class formation. Scott’s proposed historicization is not a consensus or a demand to abandon experience.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

strands.title: Bandit narratives, political power and local research
strands.focus: Hobsbawm’s revised model responds to myth and patronage objections and draws on Colombian scholarship. Songs are mediated evidence; political actors and social settings cannot be inferred directly from heroic stories.
strands.works: Bandits (1969; revised edition 2000); Sánchez/Meertens (1987)

strands.title: Migration and the timing of observation
strands.focus: Ferrie’s response to Thernstrom asks who disappears from a local sample and what happens before its first observation. His male immigrant sample does not represent every worker or family.
strands.works: Ferrie (1996 manuscript),1–8,21

strands.title: Culture under capitalism: continuity or reworking?
strands.focus: Chakrabarty rejects deriving workers’ culture from economic function alone. Nair asks whether describing traditions as survivals makes them too fixed, and how their reworking within capitalism should enter the explanation.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989/2000), preface xi–xv; Nair review (1990), 98

strands.title: Separate spheres: categories, chronology and regional evidence
strands.focus: Davidoff and Hall connect class formation to gender and familial support. Vickery values their detailed research but questions its chronology and generalization: her Lancashire comparison crosses land and trade, while prescriptive language does not straightforwardly establish women’s confinement.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987), prologue opening; Vickery (1993), 393–401

strands.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
strands.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
strands.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield participate in debate about politics within social history. The verified article metadata establishes this intervention; no detailed account of its unread argument is supplied. Scott’s 2000 reply to a later Eley–Nield essay, known through its abstract, objects that insisting on class forecloses other political categories.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored

culture.label: New cultural history
culture.description: Meaning, symbols, rituals, representation, and practices help constitute social life. Draws on anthropology and multiple historical traditions.
culture.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis; Lynn Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989), whose “Models for Cultural History” are Foucault (O’Brien), Thompson and Davis (Desan), Geertz (Biersack), and White and LaCapra (Kramer).

representative_people.context: Class is a historical relationship formed through material experience and culture; the Making preface explicitly restricts its study to English developments.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

representative_people.context: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with anthropology used for questions tested on historical evidence (1971–75). Hunt’s 1989 volume makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ a model for cultural history in Desan’s chapter.
representative_people.works: “The Reasons of Misrule” (1971); “The Rites of Violence” (1973); Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Women on the Margins (1995), selected passages

representative_people.context: Brings plural cultural approaches into debate while investigating political symbols and practices alongside a sociology of revolutionary politics.
representative_people.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984); The New Cultural History (1989), editor and introduction author; Inventing Human Rights (2007), per its reviewers

representative_people.context: An anthropological resource, not a historian’s membership in a school.
representative_people.works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973)

representative_people.context: Reading depends on material forms and differentiated practices. Collective representations help explain social divisions; critical fidelity to Annales includes disagreement with Braudel’s hierarchy.
representative_people.works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987, contextual reference cited in the article); « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003)

representative_people.context: Uses cricket and autobiographical social experience to investigate culture and aesthetics.
representative_people.works: Beyond a Boundary (1963)

representative_people.context: Chartier explicitly uses McKenzie’s account of the meanings produced by textual forms; conceptual resource, not membership in one historical school.
representative_people.works: Bibliography and the Sociology of Texts (1986; Panizzi Lectures 1985), cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Chartier uses Marin’s analysis of signs and representation in examining the relation between absent objects, present images and conventions of recognition.
representative_people.works: La critique du discours: Étude sur la Logique de Port-Royal et les Pensées de Pascal (1975), discussed by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: The meeting of text and reader supplies Chartier a resource; he also differentiates historically situated appropriation from a universal account of self-understanding.
representative_people.works: Temps et récit, vol. III, Le temps raconté (1985), pp. 228–263 as cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interpretive communities help Chartier specify differentiated reading practices, without making all readers in a society identical.
representative_people.works: Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities (1980), pp. 1–17, cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interprets unusual documents as entry points into historical meanings; the reader can contest his interpretations, and he explicitly disclaims a representative sample.
representative_people.works: The Great Cat Massacre (1984), introduction

representative_people.context: Investigates preindustrial popular culture; his later historiographical reflection questions a simple succession of cultural approaches.
representative_people.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978); “From Cultural History to Histories of Cultures” (undated electronic essay)

representative_people.context: Feminist analysis supplies a formative cultural-history resource in Hunt’s account and a directly acknowledged social/textual resource for Spiegel.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), draft and p. 101 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.context: Treats gender and experience as historical questions, joining cultural and institutional interpretation.
representative_people.works: “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Examines historical uses of Foucault. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Michel Foucault’s History of Culture, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reconsiders community and ritual through conflict and gender. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Crowds, Community, and Ritual in the Work of E. P. Thompson and Natalie Davis, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: An anthropologist comparing interpretive resources and structure/event questions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Local Knowledge, Local History: Geertz and Beyond, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes literary resources in White and LaCapra. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Literature, Criticism, and Historical Imagination: The Literary Challenge of Hayden White and Dominick LaCapra, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reads parades as changing representations of social divisions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: The American Parade: Representations of the Nineteenth-Century Social Order, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Investigates narratives that make suffering a humanitarian concern. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Bodies, Details, and the Humanitarian Narrative, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Studies visual attention beyond a simple language analogy. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Compares connoisseurship prescriptions with administrative classifications of possessions.
representative_people.works: Superfluous Things (1991), chapter 2 excerpt

representative_people.context: Studies contested authentication and the narratives accompanying transferred relics.
representative_people.works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),186–190

representative_people.context: Hunt’s The New Cultural History (1989) opens its “Models for Cultural History” with O’Brien’s chapter on Foucault, which reads his work as an alternative model for the history of culture and a critique of Marxist, Annaliste and social-historical analysis. A model offered to cultural historians, not membership of a school; his discourse, genealogy and power contexts in other entries remain distinct.
representative_people.works: Histoire de la folie (1961); Discipline and Punish (1975); The History of Sexuality I (1976)

culture.scope_note: Anthropological interpretation, historical representations, and class/cultural experience are distinct resources; culture does not arrive after material explanation ends.

strands.title: Class, conflict and cultural experience
strands.focus: Culture helps constitute social relationships in early Marxist and Caribbean inquiries; later cultural history does not inaugurate attention to meaning.
strands.works: The Making (1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963)

strands.title: Anthropological interpretation and its disputes
strands.focus: Historical interpretation adapts anthropology while debating coherence, differences and what documents permit.
strands.works: “The Rites of Violence” (1973); The Great Cat Massacre (1984); The New Cultural History (1989)

strands.title: Gender, community and conflict
strands.focus: Gender contributes to cultural inquiry and complicates unified pictures of communities and rituals.
strands.works: Gender (1986); The Body Politic and Desan chapter (1989)

strands.title: Material texts and differentiated readers
strands.focus: Textual form, circulation and appropriation help explain meanings and social divisions.
strands.works: Le monde comme représentation (1989)

strands.title: Political symbols and public performance
strands.focus: Symbols, practices and public displays enter political and social explanation.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class (1984); The American Parade (1989)

strands.title: Narrative, criticism and humanitarian concern
strands.focus: Narrative form is both a problem of historical writing and a historical object.
strands.works: Kramer and Laqueur chapters (1989); Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

strands.title: Visual practice and attention
strands.focus: Seeing and situated attention need examination beyond a simple analogy between images and language.
strands.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince (1989)

strands.title: Popular cultures and historical plurality
strands.focus: Popular culture is a historical subject with variable practices, not one timeless folk essence.
strands.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978)

strands.title: Objects and textual categories
strands.focus: Clunas asks how prescriptions and inventories classify objects. Their categories shape what historians can reconstruct; surviving museum objects alone cannot supply the whole material world.
strands.works: Superfluous Things (1991), 45–53

strands.title: Discourse, power and the critique of social history
strands.focus: O’Brien presents Foucault’s history of culture as an alternative to Marxist, Annaliste and social-historical analysis. Chartier’s appropriation of his account of discourse and Scott’s use of his conception of power are recorded as separate relationships; this strand does not make them Foucauldians.
strands.works: Patricia O’Brien, “Michel Foucault’s History of Culture” (1989)

language.label: Linguistic turn / poststructuralism
language.description: Examines how language, narrative, discourse, and power shape historical knowledge and subject formation. Narrative theory, structuralist inheritances, and poststructuralist critiques overlap but are not interchangeable. This node groups debates rather than identifying one school.
language.representative_figures_and_works: Michel Foucault; Jacques Derrida; Hayden White, Metahistory (1973). Richard Rorty, ed.: The Linguistic Turn (1967).

representative_people.context: Discourse, genealogy and subject formation are related, changing inquiries; institutional and practical relations enter the account. Historians adapt and criticize them in different ways.
representative_people.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971); “The Subject and Power” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions conceptual hierarchies and conditions of signification through close reading and institutional questions; no mechanical rule permits arbitrary interpretation.
representative_people.works: Of Grammatology (1967); “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

representative_people.context: Historical narrative theory; not every position under the linguistic turn.
representative_people.works: Metahistory (1973); The Content of the Form (1987); Figural Realism (1999); The Practical Past (2014)

representative_people.context: Reworks signification and unconscious interpretation; the linguistic turn is not a uniform Lacanian program.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Écrits collection (1966)

representative_people.context: Theorizes material ideology and the constitution of subjects; reception is specifically documented through Hall and cultural-studies debates.
representative_people.works: “Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses” (1970); Hall, “Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms” (1980)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor in historians’ reception of Foucault, organizing debate across theoretical and empirical approaches. The edited volume is not one uniform Foucauldian program.
representative_people.works: Foucault and the Writing of History, edited collection (1994); Console and Classify (1987)

representative_people.context: Derrida examines the relation of writing to the historicity of ideal objects through Husserl’s geometry. This is a particular critical engagement, not Husserl’s membership in a later historical turn.
representative_people.works: Husserl’s Origin of Geometry as discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), chapter 2 opening

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly identifies Destruktion and Abbau as resources that he adapts; the acknowledgment does not imply endorsement of Heidegger’s whole philosophy or politics.
representative_people.works: Derrida, “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly draws on signs and interpretants while questioning a final meaning outside signification. This contextual use does not equate pragmatism with deconstruction.
representative_people.works: Peirce passages discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), corrected English edition pp. 48–50

representative_people.context: An explicit resource in Foucault’s genealogy and Barthes’s discussion of facts and meaning; their appropriations are distinct from Nietzsche’s full argument.
representative_people.works: Genealogy (1887), selected passages; Foucault’s genealogy essay (1971); Barthes’s history essay (1967)

representative_people.context: Moves among myth analysis, historical discourse and a challenge to authorial closure. His trajectory is not a single timeless structuralist method.
representative_people.works: Mythologies (1957); “The Discourse of History” and “The Death of the Author” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Explicitly cited for dialogue among texts and paragrammatism in Barthes’s historical-discourse analysis. The original article is not newly read and the acknowledgment does not establish identical positions.
representative_people.works: “Bakhtine, le mot, le dialogue et le roman” (1967), cited in Barthes’s “The Discourse of History,” note 3

representative_people.context: Barthes invokes his research on ambiguous words in Greek tragedy to distinguish characters’ understanding from the spectator’s. This is a named scholarly resource, not a formal linguistic-turn affiliation.
representative_people.works: Research on Greek tragedy as invoked in “The Death of the Author” (1967), final paragraph

representative_people.context: A historian and translator who makes rhetorical analysis usable for historiography while retaining questions about sources and reference.
representative_people.works: Barthes translation (1981); “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983/1990)

representative_people.context: Reads texts as situated social acts with distinct discursive forms; manuscript and patronage evidence changed her initial hypothesis.
representative_people.works: Romancing the Past (1993), introduction, acknowledgments and notes

representative_people.context: Historicizes gender categories and the production of experience while retaining institutional relations and historical inquiry.
representative_people.works: “Gender” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Questions the political idioms through which class receives meaning; this is a particular historical intervention.
representative_people.works: Languages of Class (1983), selected introduction opening

representative_people.context: Reconsiders textual interpretation and the meaning of context through literary criticism and philosophy.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

representative_people.context: Investigates laboring people’s understandings of social order across politics, work, language and art.
representative_people.works: Visions of the People (1991)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor whose article explicitly frames meaning and experience as a historiographical problem; detailed argument remains to be checked.
representative_people.works: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987)

representative_people.context: Spiegel explicitly credits her draft argument and sustained manuscript reading in developing a social/textual historical method.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), cited in Romancing the Past (1993), introduction note 7

representative_people.context: Socially situated discourse is an explicitly cited resource for Spiegel, not a formal affiliation with a later historians’ school.
representative_people.works: The Dialogic Imagination (English 1981), p. 259 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.context: White explicitly adapts a literary taxonomy while allowing alternatives.
representative_people.works: Anatomy of Criticism (1957)

representative_people.context: Named rhetorical resource in White’s introduction; distinct from Peter Burke and Edmund Burke III.
representative_people.works: A Grammar of Motives (edition cited by White1969)

representative_people.context: White discusses representation through a comparison with literary inquiry.
representative_people.works: Mimesis, cited by White in Metahistory (1973),2n1

representative_people.context: Develops a feminist response to Scott’s treatment of experience and agency.
representative_people.works: “Feminist History after the Linguistic Turn” (1994), 374–379

representative_people.context: Rorty’s anthology of analytic philosophers’ essays on philosophical method gave the phrase “the linguistic turn” wide currency. Historians’ linguistic turn drew mainly on other, often French, resources, so this records the name’s source, not a lineage.
representative_people.works: The Linguistic Turn (1967), ed.

representative_people.context: Criticised the linguistic turn in social history as a 'reification of language' (Descent into Discourse, 1990, as quoted by Callinicos, 1992), while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'; Scott answered him in 1987 that class struggle is produced in discourse.
representative_people.works: “Response to Joan Scott” (1987); Descent into Discourse (1990)

representative_people.context: Holds that practices are not reducible to discourse and that social positions are conditions of possibility of discourse; in 2003 he described cultural historians as having moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. His questions to Hayden White (1993) are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder.
representative_people.works: « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003), ¶25–26, 31; “Quatre questions à Hayden White” (1993), as White restates them (1995)

strands.title: Discourse and genealogy
strands.focus: Archaeology examines rules connecting actual statements and the formation of objects; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Social and institutional relations enter these inquiries.
strands.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), three chapters; “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971), pp. 139–152

strands.title: Deconstruction
strands.focus: Critical work through conceptual hierarchies and differential relations, with an explicitly adapted Heidegger resource. The 1983 letter rejects a mechanical method and includes institutions and translation.
strands.works: Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2; “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983)

strands.title: Narrative theory
strands.focus: Emplotment and tropes concern the forms of historical explanation.
strands.works: Metahistory

strands.title: Signification and divided subjectivity
strands.focus: Lacan’s changed sign diagram and reading of dream-work distinguish his appropriation from literal repetition of Saussure. Historians debate its capacity to explain changing gender relations.
strands.works: “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Scott, “Gender” (1986)

strands.title: Ideology, practices and subjects
strands.focus: Althusser’s interpellation operates through material practices. His apparatuses include contradiction and resistance; Hall’s adoption and criticism remain a specific reception.
strands.works: “Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses” (1970); Hall (1980)

strands.title: Subject formation, action and resistance
strands.focus: Foucault distinguishes power relations from capacities and communication while studying their interconnections; freedom and resistance enter action upon actions. Goldstein provides a historically situated interlocutor.
strands.works: “The Subject and Power” (1982); Foucault and the Writing of History (1994)

strands.title: Writing, ideal objects and historicity
strands.focus: Derrida’s critical reading of Husserl asks how writing enters the historical transmission of ideal objects. It is distinct from a claim that historical evidence has no constraints.
strands.works: Of Grammatology (1967), chapter 2 opening

strands.title: Interpretants and a critique of presence
strands.focus: Peirce is a named resource in Derrida’s account of signification; this particular use neither subsumes all pragmatism nor equates arbitrariness with individual caprice.
strands.works: Of Grammatology, corrected English edition (1997), pp. 44–50

strands.title: Madness, reason and discursive practice
strands.focus: Derrida questions the language of an archaeology of silence; Foucault disputes his reading of Descartes and the reduction of discursive practices to textual traces. Each criticism remains attributed.
strands.works: “Cogito and the History of Madness” (lecture 1963); “My Body, This Paper, This Fire” (English 1979)

strands.title: Genealogical questions and perspectival knowledge
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s distinction between origins and uses, and his account of multiple perspectives, enter different later arguments in Foucault and Barthes. Their readings are not interchangeable.
strands.works: Genealogy II.12–13 and III.12; Foucault (1971); Barthes (1967)

strands.title: Myth and the naturalization of history
strands.focus: Barthes’s two-level account asks how historically produced meanings appear natural. He links formal analysis with historical criticism, rather than treating semiology as sufficient by itself.
strands.works: “Myth Today” (1957), selected passages

strands.title: Authorship, textual plurality and the reader
strands.focus: The 1967 essay questions the author as final explanatory authority and invokes Vernant’s tragic ambiguity. Its theoretical reader must be distinguished from research on actual readers.
strands.works: “The Death of the Author” (1967), Richard Howard translation

strands.title: Historical utterance, reference and narrative detail
strands.focus: Barthes distinguishes acts of uttering, content units and signification, drawing on Jakobson and Kristeva. Bann’s adoption and qualification keep historical practice within the debate.
strands.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: Social sites and textual action
strands.focus: Spiegel combines attention to form with documentary and patronage inquiry; texts act in social settings and are not transparent reflections.
strands.works: Romancing the Past (1993), introduction

strands.title: Gender categories and historical experience
strands.focus: Scott makes experience something to explain and connects meanings with institutions and subjectivity.
strands.works: Gender (1986); The Evidence of Experience (1991)

strands.title: Class and political idioms
strands.focus: Different historical inquiries question how social identities receive political meaning.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); Visions of the People (1991)

strands.title: Texts, contexts and debates over experience
strands.focus: LaCapra’s textual/contextual project and Toews’s explicitly titled meaning/experience intervention are distinct; detailed agreement is not presumed.
strands.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn (1987)

strands.title: Literary taxonomies and historical events
strands.focus: White distinguishes narrative arrangement from invented events and treats plot classifications as revisable analytical choices.
strands.works: Metahistory (1973),1–11

language.scope_note: Structural linguistics, discourse, deconstruction, and narrative theory differ. A historical concern with language alone does not identify a poststructuralist.

global.description: Moves across national containers through comparison, interaction, circulation, and connections. These approaches differ; global scale need not imply one theory of globalization.

representative_people.context: World synthesis and an explicit account of historical interpretation; source criticism and better-fitting accounts remain valuable within his ecumenical program.

labourhistory.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.
